## Simple explanation

Representation learning lets a model discover useful ways to describe
examples instead of requiring people to hand-design every feature. For
images, a representation might encode edges and shapes; for text, it might
capture aspects of meaning and context.

## Technical explanation

A representation is a mapping from input data to a feature vector or
structured latent state. The mapping is learned through supervised,
self-supervised, contrastive, or generative objectives. A useful
representation preserves information relevant to downstream tasks while
discarding nuisance variation.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Learned representations power transfer learning, similarity search,
classification, and multimodal systems. Their quality depends on training
data and objectives, and an embedding that works for one use may not work
well for another.

## How it works

An encoder maps examples to representations, and a training objective
encourages desired properties such as predicting labels, reconstructing
inputs, or bringing related pairs closer. Downstream systems consume the
learned features directly or fine-tune the encoder.

## Practical example

A vision encoder pretrained on images can convert product photos into
vectors. A downstream classifier can use these features or fine-tune the
encoder on labeled examples from a particular catalog.

## Common misconceptions

- A compact or visually meaningful embedding is not automatically useful
  for every downstream task.
- Representation similarity is determined by the learned geometry and
  metric; it should be validated against the intended notion of similarity.
